bullets.label: Student Learning Notes · Advanced Pathway for Internationally Qualified Nurses

cards.title: Welcome to Level 3
cards.body: Global Nursing Professionals do more than follow safety procedures. At this level, you will lead improvements, analyse patterns of harm, strengthen systems and help create environments where safety is a shared organisational value.

bullets.label: Champion safety, openness and continuous learning
Design, evaluate and improve quality initiatives
Lead a culture of safety, openness and continuous learning
Analyse incidents using systems and human-factors approaches
Use surveillance data to strengthen infection prevention
Apply digital technologies safely and ethically
Lead preparedness for outbreaks, disasters and emerging risks

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: Healthcare harm rarely results from one person's action alone. It arises from weaknesses in communication, workflow, technology, staffing, policy and organisational culture.

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals recognise these
bullets.text: Global Nursing Professionals recognise these connections and lead practical improvements that make safe practice easier for everyone.

bullets.label: Your goal: lead safety and quality initiatives,
bullets.text: Your goal: lead safety and quality initiatives, use data and evidence to improve systems, support colleagues and contribute to safer healthcare — locally and globally.

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: Leading a Culture of Safety & Psychological Safety

bullets.label: Safety culture reflects the values and
bullets.text: Safety culture reflects the values and behaviours that determine how an organisation responds to risk, error and improvement. Nurse leaders influence culture through their daily actions.

Communicate that safety is a priority — even under pressure

bullets.text: Makes it normal to report hazards, question unsafe decisions and learn from incidents. Supported by staffing, equipment, education and visible leadership.

bullets.text: Team members can ask questions, admit uncertainty and raise concerns without fear of humiliation. Enables early communication to prevent or correct mistakes.

bullets.label: Distinguishes human error, at-risk behaviour
bullets.text: Distinguishes human error, at-risk behaviour and recklessness. Automatic blame discourages reporting; absence of accountability also damages safety.

bullets.label: Strengthen trust by responding promptly,
bullets.text: Strengthen trust by responding promptly, following through on concerns and explaining decisions. Staff notice when safety messages are not matched by action.

bullets.text: Nurses also contribute to antimicrobial stewardship by preventing infection and supporting appropriate use of antimicrobial medicines.

Infection or fall rates — what happened

decks.title: Leading a Culture of Safety and Psychological Safety
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 2 - Level 3 - Section 1 - Global Nurse Professional - Presentation deck.pptx

bullets.label: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments — Section 1: Leading a Culture of Safety and Psychological Safety

cards.title: What Is Safety Culture?
cards.body: Safety culture reflects the shared values and behaviours that determine how an organisation responds to risk, error, and improvement.

bullets.label: A strong safety culture makes it normal — and expected — to:
Policies must be matched by staffing, equipment, education, and visible leadership behaviour.

cards.title: The Role of Nurse Leaders in Shaping Culture

bullets.label: Respond to concerns promptly and without dismissal.
Match your response to behaviour, not just outcomes.
Demonstrate the behaviours you expect from your team every day.
Treat every incident as an opportunity to improve systems.

cards.title: Psychological Safety in Healthcare Teams
cards.body: Psychological safety means team members have the confidence to speak up — to ask questions, admit uncertainty, and raise concerns — without fear of humiliation or punishment.

bullets.label: It is not the absence of accountability. It is
bullets.text: It is not the absence of accountability. It is the foundation for early communication that prevents mistakes before they reach patients.

bullets.label: Teams with high psychological safety report errors earlier and recover faster.

cards.title: Understanding Just Culture
cards.body: A just culture distinguishes between three types of behaviour when responding to incidents:

bullets.label: Unintentional mistake — requires system redesign and support, not blame.
Shortcuts taken without full awareness of risk — requires coaching and removal of incentives for unsafe shortcuts.
Conscious disregard for risk — requires proportionate accountability.
Automatic blame discourages reporting. A
bullets.text: Automatic blame discourages reporting. A complete absence of accountability also damages safety. Just culture seeks the balance.

cards.title: Why Just Culture Matters for NCLEX Candidates
cards.body: NCLEX tests your ability to prioritise patient safety above all else

bullets.label: Questions on incident response assess knowledge of error classification and escalation pathways
Understanding just culture helps you select answers that reflect systemic thinking, not reactive blame

cards.title: Clinical Example: Feeding Tube Incident
cards.body: A junior nurse realises she has connected a feeding tube incorrectly — and identifies it before patient use.

bullets.label: Root cause identified: Confusing connectors and interruptions during preparation.
Team action: Introduced a standard setup
bullets.text: Team action: Introduced a standard setup protocol and simulation practice — treating this as a system issue, not individual carelessness.

cards.title: Leadership Presence: Turning Words Into Action

bullets.label: Always act on reported concerns — staff notice when nothing changes.
Transparency about outcomes builds trust in the reporting process.
Regular presence on the floor reinforces that safety is lived, not just stated.
Safety culture is not built in a single
bullets.text: Safety culture is not built in a single intervention. It is reinforced every time a leader responds to a concern with fairness, curiosity, and visible action.

bullets.label: Create an environment where raising concerns is expected and valued.
Match accountability to the behaviour and its context — not just the outcome.
Ask what in the system allowed an error to occur, not only who made it.
Safety culture is visible only when leaders act on every concern raised.
NCLEX Tip: When answering safety and leadership
bullets.text: NCLEX Tip: When answering safety and leadership questions, always look for the option that addresses the system first and supports team communication.

decks.title: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 2 - Level 3 - Section 2 - Global Nurse Professional - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Systems Thinking & Human Factors in Nursing
cards.body: Section 2 · Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) — Programme 2: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Move beyond individual blame to understand the full chain of events.
Recognise human and system factors that contribute to unsafe conditions.
Use contributory-factor frameworks to investigate incidents systematically.
Propose practical, evidence-based system improvements to reduce risk.

cards.title: What Is Systems Thinking?
cards.body: When an error occurs, the visible action is rarely the whole story. A longer chain of conditions — staffing gaps, look-alike packaging, poor lighting, interruptions, or unclear responsibilities — may all contribute.

bullets.label: The observable event or near miss.
The sequence of actions and decisions.
The underlying system factors that created the opportunity for error.
Memory, attention and perception are all
bullets.text: Memory, attention and perception are all finite. Safe systems are designed around normal human limitations — not perfect performance.

cards.title: Hierarchy of Controls
cards.body: Not all safety measures are equally effective. Stronger controls make safe actions the default — not just the intended action.

bullets.label: Education and reminders alone are often the
bullets.text: Education and reminders alone are often the weakest control. Prioritise elimination, substitution and redesign wherever possible.

bullets.label: Effective incident reviews must include those
bullets.text: Effective incident reviews must include those who understand the work — frontline nurses, clinical staff and, where appropriate, patients and families.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Wrong-Selection Medication Errors
cards.body: A ward experiences repeated errors involving two injectable medicines with similar packaging stored side by side. A systems review reveals multiple contributing factors — not a single individual mistake.

bullets.label: Both medicines stored next to each other, increasing selection confusion.
Look-alike packaging with insufficient visual differentiation between products.
Staff distracted during preparation, reducing attentional accuracy.
Search results displayed both drug names together, prompting confusion at the point of selection.
Each intervention targeted a specific
bullets.text: Each intervention targeted a specific contributing factor — moving from weaker (education alone) to stronger (engineering and system redesign) controls to sustainably reduce risk.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Look for Conditions, Not Just Actions

bullets.label: Seek the system factors that shaped the error — not just the final act.
Build processes that support — not punish — human cognitive constraints.
Reminders and training are weak when used alone. Prioritise redesign and engineering safeguards.
Evaluate whether changes actually reduce risk. Learning is a cycle, not a one-off event.

decks.title: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 2 - Level 3 - Section 3 - Global Nurse Professional - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Quality Improvement, Surveillance & Antimicrobial Stewardship
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 2 · Level 3

cards.title: What You Will Learn
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Use data to identify a safety or infection-prevention issue clearly before acting.
Use a structured quality-improvement approach to test and refine change.
Distinguish between process, outcome and balancing measures.
Explain the nurse's contribution to antimicrobial stewardship and infection prevention.

cards.title: Introduction: Data-Driven Nursing Practice
cards.body: Global Nursing Professionals use data to identify patterns, test improvements and evaluate outcomes. Everyday observations — infection trends, incident reports, patient feedback — become organised learning when captured systematically. Nurses are central to turning data into safer care.

bullets.label: Improvement begins by defining a specific problem and understanding current practice. Teams then:
Adapt the intervention based on evidence
Small tests of change allow learning before wider implementation — reducing risk and building confidence.
The PDSA cycle is the foundation of structured
bullets.text: The PDSA cycle is the foundation of structured quality improvement. Each completed cycle generates evidence to refine the next iteration, enabling safe, incremental progress towards measurable goals.

bullets.label: What actually happened — e.g., infection rates, fall rates, length of stay. Shows the impact of care.
Whether recommended care occurred — e.g., hand-hygiene compliance, timely device review. Shows delivery of care.
Unintended consequences — e.g., delays, increased workload, need for reinsertion. Prevents harm shifting.
Always measure across all three categories. A
bullets.text: Always measure across all three categories. A successful outcome measure means little if balancing measures reveal new harms.

bullets.label: Surveillance identifies trends by location,
bullets.text: Surveillance identifies trends by location, organism, procedure or device. It turns routine data into actionable intelligence — but only when the data are:

bullets.label: Communicated to those who can act
Used to support improvement, not just report performance

cards.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship: The Nurse's Role
cards.body: Nurses are on the front line of stewardship — every shift, every patient.

bullets.label: Accurate specimens before antimicrobials start — ensuring targeted therapy.
Give antimicrobials at the prescribed time to maintain therapeutic levels.
Check allergy status, monitor response, and challenge unnecessary continuation through appropriate channels.
Explain why completing treatment matters and the risks of antimicrobial resistance.
A ward records a rise in catheter-associated
bullets.text: A ward records a rise in catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs). The improvement team maps the process and discovers catheter necessity is not reviewed consistently.

bullets.label: Daily catheter necessity review prompt introduced
Feedback dashboard created for the team
Clearly identify the problem and understand current practice before choosing an intervention.
Track both outcome and process measures — and always check for unintended consequences.
Data should reach the people who can act on it, in time to make a difference.
Every infection prevented is an antimicrobial not needed. Prevention and stewardship are inseparable.

decks.title: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 2 - Level 3 - Section 4 - Global Nurse Professional - Presentation deck.pptx

bullets.label: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration

cards.title: Section 4 Overview
cards.body: Why Digital Safety Matters in Modern Nursing

bullets.label: Modern nursing extends well beyond the physical
bullets.text: Modern nursing extends well beyond the physical ward. Electronic records, clinical decision support tools, remote monitoring and connected devices can transform care quality — but they also introduce new and complex risks.

bullets.label: Global Nursing Professionals must use
bullets.text: Global Nursing Professionals must use technology critically and responsibly, protect patient information, and contribute to preparedness for outbreaks, disasters and emerging health threats.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Recognise both the opportunities and hazards of digital healthcare systems in clinical settings.
Apply best practices for electronic records, connected devices and information governance.
Contribute meaningfully to outbreak and emergency preparedness plans.
Share learning across organisations and countries to strengthen healthcare systems worldwide.
Nurses must verify critical information and report technology-related hazards promptly.
Patient information must be accessed only for
bullets.text: Patient information must be accessed only for legitimate care purposes. Digital convenience does not diminish the duty of confidentiality — it demands even greater vigilance.

bullets.label: Use strong, unique credentials and never share login details.
Position screens appropriately and lock devices when unattended.
Use only approved channels when sharing patient data digitally.

cards.title: Preparedness and Resilience
cards.body: Outbreaks and disasters cannot wait for a plan to be created. Preparedness must be built before an emergency begins.

bullets.label: Every team member knows their responsibilities during an emergency response.
Established chains of communication ensure rapid, accurate information flow.
Adequate PPE availability and triage processes protect staff and patients alike.
Regular drills and education embed preparedness into everyday culture.

cards.title: Global Collaboration in Nursing
cards.body: Infection and safety threats do not respect borders. Global Nursing Professionals play a vital role in strengthening international responses.

bullets.label: Contribute data to outbreak monitoring networks and WHO-aligned systems.
Apply global best practices within the context of local resources and culture.
Avoid assuming one solution fits every setting — local knowledge is essential.
During a respiratory outbreak, a hospital
bullets.text: During a respiratory outbreak, a hospital introduces remote monitoring to reduce unnecessary room entry. Nurse leaders quickly identify that alarm thresholds are generating too many non-urgent alerts — a classic case of alert fatigue.

bullets.label: They collaborate with clinicians and technical
bullets.text: They collaborate with clinicians and technical staff to recalibrate the system, maintain direct assessment for concerning patients, and establish a clear downtime plan.

bullets.label: Technology supports care — it does not replace professional judgement.
Clinical judgement remains central. Use digital tools critically and verify all critical information.
Every digital interaction is governed by the same duty of confidentiality as face-to-face care.
Planning, regular simulation, and workforce support build true resilience before crises emerge.
Engage with international networks — and always adapt solutions to fit local needs and resources.

cards.title: End-of-Programme Summary
cards.body: By completing GNPS Programme 2 – Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional.

bullets.label: Champion safety and quality in every environment you work in.
Use data and critical thinking to identify and address risks.
Embrace technology while preserving the primacy of clinical judgement.
Protect patients and the workforce through knowledge, courage and collaboration.
Protecting patients and protecting the
bullets.text: Protecting patients and protecting the workforce are shared responsibilities — requiring knowledge, courage, collaboration and continuous learning.
